newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shanghai Petrochem faces tough year ahead.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Petrochem faces tough year ahead.

text.p: Shanghai Petrochemical Co Ltd will continue to face poor demand, soft sales prices for most of its products and high raw material costs in 1997, senior company officials said on Tuesday.
However, they also said they did not see further decline in prices for their oil and petrochemical products.

"Though the petrochemical industry in China has to continue to fight a weak domestic market in the short run, the company believes that further declines of the current low product pricing are unlikely," said president Wu Yixin.

The H share company announced a 52.6 percent fall in profit attributable to shareholders to 1.01 billion yuan in 1996 from 2.13 billion yuan in previous year, according to international accounting standards.
This was substantially below the HK$1.52 billion consensus forecast of Hong Kong analysts covering the company.
Turnover rose to 11.90 billion yuan from 11.83 billion yuan in 1995.
The company also announced a cut in its final dividend per share to 0.08 yuan per share, compared with a 1995 final dividend of 0.09 per share. The total payout for 1996 was 0.12 yuan per share.

The company faces several challenges in 1997. It will be seeking ways to offset the negative effects of a shutdown of its facilities for regular maintenance and projected crude oil price increases, president Wu said.
"The cost of crude oil for the company in 1997 will be higher than that in 1996," said Wu.
The cost of crude oil is crucial to the company's profitability, since crude accounted for 47.7 percent of the company's total production cost in 1996.

In 1996, the weighted average price of crude oil, including that sourced domestically and imported oil, was 997 yuan per tonne, an increase of 20.1 percent over 1995 average, a company statement said.
About 56 percent of the company's output is synthetic fibres and resins and plastics. The remaining 44 percent is intermediate petrochemicals and petroleum products.
While demand for synthetic fibres and resins is forecast to remain weak, the company will seek to increase its production of higher-value petroleum products.
"The company is seeking to increase the import of high quality crude oil so as to sustain the competitiveness of its products," Wu said.
To this end the company is building a new crude oil wharf at Cezi Island in Zhoushan, Zhejiang province.
The company will try to increase earnings from producing more high-value products, such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
In 1997, the company will initiate a two-tier inspection and maintenance programme on its production facilities
Overhaul of production facilities built in phase one and two was scheduled for the first-half of 1997, said Wu.
Those built in phase three, including an ethylene unit will be undertaken toward the end of 1997 or early 1998, Wu added.

Weak short-term demand for the company's products has not slowed its expansion plans. The company's 300,000-tonne ethylene plant is being expanded by 100,000 tonnes and completion is expected in early 1998.

A 100,000-tonne low density polyethylene (LDPE) project through its joint venture, Shanghai Golden Phillips Company Ltd, is currently installing equipment. It would be completed by end 1997 and trial production will begin in early 1998, said Wu.
